h.strategy: Use retrieved findings to judge which settings are strong, weak or neutral, and which parts other settings can cut off from the outcome. Build hypotheses mainly from (a) the edited field's current parent value: replacing a strong value with a weak one hurts, and filling an empty or harmful slot helps; and (b) conditions that disconnect the edited part, pushing its effect toward zero. Directions refer to the signed effect, not its size. Disconnection makes the effect lower only if the edit usually helps, and higher if it usually hurts. If the usual sign is unclear, do not use it. When finding flaws, check this sign logic first. Replace any hypothesis whose direction could reverse through a competing effect or that relies on partial redundancy. Vary edit fields and values. State a one-sentence mechanism.

hyps.why: Edge 0 being empty leaves node 1 without input, so a conv there revives two dead paths with a large gain.
Adding a conv to an empty edge into the output gives more gain than swapping an already useful op.
With edge 0 none, node 1 gets no input, so the conv on edge 4 is cut off and its usual gain vanishes.
With edge 5 none, node 2 has no route to the output, so the conv on edge 2 is disconnected and has no effect.
Edge 1 only reaches the output through edge 5, so with edge 5 none a conv on edge 1 is disconnected and its gain vanishes.
With edge 0 none, node 1 is empty, so a conv on edge 2 carries nothing and its gain vanishes.
With edge 0 none, node 1 is empty and edge 4 is already dead, so deleting it costs nothing whereas it normally costs accuracy.
With edge 5 none, edge 1 is already disconnected from the output, so deleting it costs nothing whereas it usually costs accuracy.
Filling an empty slot with a strong conv adds a whole path, whereas replacing an existing op yields a smaller gain.
Removing a strong conv feeding the output costs more accuracy than removing a weak op.
